events.text: A clear night after the first frost, and you wake on the summit with the cold in your fur and something wrong with your stripes. They are not black any more. They are night, deep and blue, and in them, along your flanks and your neck and the root of your tail, there are stars. The magpie lands on the pine above you, cocks its head, and begins to read you aloud, mansion by mansion, the way a clerk reads out a ledger to a magistrate who is not going to like it.

choices.text: Lie still and let it read

effects.log: Legs, Bond, Stomach, Hairy Head, Net, Turtle Beak, Three Stars. Where a case was judged justly the stars are lit. Where it was not, the stripe is bare white, like a page nobody wrote on. The magpie reads the bare ones twice, louder.

choices.text: Ask the magpie whether a bare stripe can still be filled

effects.log: The magpie laughs, which is its answer to most things. Then it says, quite seriously: "A case is a case. The mountain does not run out of them." It flies off to find you one.

choices.text: Shake yourself, as if the stars were snow

effects.log: The stars stay. Three villages see a tiger made of night walking along the ridge, and the woodcutters stop crossing the pass after dark for a whole generation.

events.text: The bare stripe of Legs, the Great Boar, the star of ditches and drains. Below the pass two villages share one irrigation ditch, and in a dry summer the upper village has dammed it with stones and turf. The lower village sends its young men up with mattocks. Blood in the ditch by noon. The magpie lands between them and points its beak at you. Before you judge, you notice: the ditch was dug, a hundred years ago, by the lower village alone.

choices.text: Break the dam: the water belongs to the ones who dug for it

effects.log: You pull the dam out with one paw. The upper village wails. But the ditch has the lower village's name in it, every stone, and the star of Legs lights along your flank like a lamp somebody finally remembered.

choices.text: Split the water by day and by night, and pardon both

effects.log: The lower village takes the day, the upper the night, and the headmen swear on the ditch. It is mercy, and it is also fair, since nobody bled to death. The star of Legs lights, a little dimmer than it might have, but lit.

choices.text: Punish the young men with mattocks

effects.log: You drive the lower village's young men home bleeding. They were the ones with the right. The stripe of Legs stays bare, and the magpie writes nothing down, very pointedly.

events.text: The bare stripe of Bond, the star of the gathering of crowds. A famine market in the town under the mountain, and a mob has broken into the house of a rice-broker and is dragging him into the street. Somebody has a rope. The broker screams that he sold at the county's price. The magpie, from the roof, tells you what the crowd does not know: the county's price was set by the broker's cousin.

choices.text: Come down into the street and stop the rope

effects.log: A white tiger in the market. The crowd goes back like a wave going out. You put a paw on the broker, and then you look at the cousin, and the crowd understands. Nobody hangs. The cousin leaves the county by morning, and the star of Bond lights.

choices.text: Let the crowd have him

effects.log: The rope goes over the beam. The cousin, who set the price, watches from a window and is never touched. The stripe of Bond stays bare: a crowd that kills the wrong man is not justice, only weather.

choices.text: Roar once, scatter them, and judge nobody

effects.log: Everyone runs, the broker included. Nothing is decided. The magpie says, kindly enough, that frightening people is not the same as judging them, and that it has said so before.

events.text: The bare stripe of Stomach, Heaven's Granary. A county magistrate has sealed the relief granary in a spring of hunger, waiting for the price to rise, and sends the starving away with a list of forms. The granary key hangs on his belt. He sleeps very well. Your hunger, tonight, is a long cold thing, and you know exactly how the starving feel.

choices.text: Open the granary and leave the magistrate to the governor

effects.log: The doors come off their pins. By morning the rice is in four hundred houses, and on the magistrate's desk there is one long white hair, laid across his seal. The governor, who also read the omen, dismisses him by noon. The star of Stomach lights.

choices.text: Eat the magistrate

effects.log: It is quick, and there are people who thank you for it. But a ghost in a magistrate's robe walks behind you on the pass from now on, reciting forms, and the stripe of Stomach stays bare: a granary is opened by hands, not teeth.

choices.text: Pardon him, if he opens it himself

ok.log: You sit at the foot of his bed until he wakes. He opens the granary at dawn with his own hands and weeps doing it. The county remembers him, afterwards, as a good magistrate, which is the cruellest thing you could have done to him. The star of Stomach lights.

fail.log: He promises everything and opens nothing, and leaves for the capital with the key. The stripe of Stomach stays bare.

events.text: The bare stripe of Hairy Head, the star of the northern horsemen and of the gathering in white. A funeral is crossing the pass: a bier, a dozen mourners in undyed hemp, a hired wailer. Halfway up, the magpie says the bier is too heavy for one old man. Under the shroud there are bows. The mourners are raiders from over the river, and the village at the foot of the pass is asleep.

choices.text: Stop the funeral at the narrows, and send them back over the river alive

effects.log: They see you in the narrows and the bows come out of the shroud. Then they see the size of you. They go back down the far side of the pass, carrying the bier, which was heavy, and the village never knows. The star of Hairy Head lights.

choices.text: Take them in the narrows, every one

ok.log: It is short and loud and the snow is red afterwards. You do not eat any of them: these were not hunger, they were judgement. The star of Hairy Head lights, and it is not a soft light.

fail.log: Twelve bows at ten paces. You come out of the narrows with arrows in you like a hedgehog, and the raiders scatter into the woods.
fail.deathCause: twelve raiders' arrows in the narrows of the pass

choices.text: Let the funeral pass. It is not your business to stop mourners

effects.log: The village burns at midnight. The stripe of Hairy Head stays bare, and every year afterwards, on that night, the magpie does not speak to you at all.

events.text: The bare stripe of Net, the hunting cart, the star of the bow and the snare. Poachers on your mountain: three brothers with wire snares, working the deer runs out of season. In one of their snares, this morning, is not a deer but a girl of ten from the village, the caught leg already blue. The brothers are arguing over whether to cut her loose or leave and say nothing.

choices.text: Free the child, and take the snares, and let the brothers run

effects.log: The wire parts like a hair under your tooth. The brothers run without their snares, and they never come back to the mountain, and the girl limps home on your back. The star of Net lights. A just pardon still takes the tools away.

choices.text: Free the child, then hunt the brothers as they hunted

effects.log: You run them down the mountain the way they ran deer, and leave all three in the river, alive and very wet and very much afraid. The village elders make them swear off the snare. The star of Net lights, hard and bright.

choices.text: Eat the brothers

effects.log: One is enough, and the other two run. The child lives. But one more ghost walks behind you now, wire-scarred, and the stripe of Net stays bare. Hunger is not a verdict.

events.text: The bare stripe of Turtle Beak, the tiger's head, the star of garrisons. A deserter from the frontier garrison has hidden in the shrine at your pass, eighteen years old, feet bleeding. Behind him, two soldiers and a sergeant with a warrant. The boy says his officer sold the garrison's winter rice and the men were eating bark. The sergeant says desertion is death. The magpie, which has been to the frontier, says both of them are telling the truth.

choices.text: Give the boy to the sergeant, and the officer to the general

effects.log: The boy goes back in ropes. The officer goes back in a cage, because a white tiger walked into the general's tent and laid the rice-ledger on his map. At the trial the boy is spared and the officer is not. The star of Turtle Beak lights.

choices.text: Hide the boy, and send the soldiers home

effects.log: The boy lives, and grows old in a village two valleys over. The officer goes on selling the rice. Other boys go on eating bark. The stripe of Turtle Beak stays bare: mercy for one is not justice for a garrison.

choices.text: Weigh it all night, and judge at dawn

ok.log: At dawn you send the sergeant to the frontier with the boy as his witness, not his prisoner. The garrison eats that winter. The star of Turtle Beak lights.

fail.log: At dawn you still do not know, and the sergeant has taken the boy while you were thinking. The stripe stays bare.

events.text: The bare stripe of the Three Stars, the White Tiger itself: the Balance above and the Punishment below. A life for a life. In the village under the pass a woman has killed her husband with a fulling club after twenty years of his fists. The county will behead her after the equinox. She has asked for nothing. Her daughter has come up the pass alone in the dark, to the shrine, and is asking the plank-painting of the old man and the tiger to do something.

choices.text: Wait for a day of rain, when no one may be executed, and speak to the magistrate

effects.log: Not on a solar term, not in rain, not before dawn. You give the county a month of soft rain, and in the month you sit in the magistrate's dreams and show him twenty years of the husband. The sentence is commuted to exile. The star of the Three Stars lights: the Balance first.

choices.text: Let the law take its course: a life was taken

effects.log: The sword falls on a dry day after the equinox. The law was obeyed, and the law was blind. The stripe of the Three Stars stays bare, because the Balance was never lifted, only the Punishment.

choices.text: Carry the daughter home and stay out of human law

effects.log: She sleeps on your back all the way down. In the morning the county does what counties do. The stripe stays bare, and so, for a long time, do you.

events.text: A winter night, and you look along your own flank and find no bare white at all. Legs, Bond, Stomach, Hairy Head, Net, Turtle Beak, Three Stars: the whole western sky is lying on the summit, breathing. The magpie reads it through once, and then, for the first time in seven hundred years, says nothing clever at all.

choices.text: Lie on the summit until dawn and let the villages see

effects.log: Every village from the pass to the river sees the western sky come down and lie on the mountain. Mothers point. Children are told what it means, which is: somebody up there is keeping count, and is fair.

choices.text: Ask the magpie why it is quiet

effects.log: "It is a long time since I read a full docket," it says. "The last one belonged to your grandmother." Then it remembers itself, and laughs at your whiskers, which have frost in them.

events.text: The old man of the mountain sends for you. The god sits under the pine, staff across the knees, a list in the lap, and does not look up. "The tiger-catching captain in the county town," says the old man. "{npc}. Paid by the size of the tiger and by who strikes first. {He} has taken eleven pelts off my mountains in nine years. Not one of them ever touched a human. The one that eats travellers on the north road, {he} leaves alone. Do you know why?"

choices.text: "Because a live man-eater keeps the bounty coming"

effects.log: The old man nods slowly. "Eleven small tigers make a good living," says the god. "One dead man-eater ends it. Break the bounty, my tiger. That is the last errand I will set you."

choices.text: "Because it is too big for {him}"

effects.log: "It is not too big for {him}," says the old man. "It is too useful." A finger taps the list. "Go and look. That is the last errand I will set you."

events.text: You go down to the county town in the shape of a grey-haired traveller and sit in the yard of the tiger-catchers' hall. {npc} keeps the ledger personally: pelts by length in hand-spans, large, middle, small, the name of whoever struck first, the silver paid. The small pelts are entered as large. The first strikes are all {npc}'s. Behind the hall a cub's pelt is drying on a frame, white at the tail-tip.

choices.text: Memorise the ledger

ok.log: Nine years of false lengths and stolen strikes. By the time the yard boy brings you tea you could recite it to the governor, and you intend to.

fail.log: The numbers swim. You get the shape of it, if not every line: enough for a tiger, not enough for a governor.

choices.text: Stand in front of the white-tipped pelt for a long time

effects.log: A hunter asks if you knew the animal. You say it was a cousin. The hunter laughs. You do not, and the laughing stops, and the hunter goes inside, and does not come out again until you have gone.

events.text: The man-eater of the north road: an old striped tiger with a broken canine, who learned forty years ago that humans are slow and has never unlearned it. Three ghosts walk ahead of it on the road at dusk, calling softly. It has smelt you coming for two days, and it is waiting on the bend where the travellers die, flattened in the bracken.

choices.text: Kill it on the bend, yourself

ok.log: It is old and it is cunning and you are a star-barred tiger seven hundred years old. It is over before the ghosts have finished their call. Afterwards the three ghosts stand in the road looking at the body, as if not sure where to go.

fail.log: It goes for your throat out of the bracken with forty years of practice behind it, and your hide holds by a hair. It is old; you are older. When the bracken stops moving the man-eater is dead, and so nearly are you. (-28 health)
fail.deathCause: the man-eater of the north road, on the bend where the travellers die

choices.text: Drive it into the open, where the tiger-catchers must take it

effects.log: You herd it down off the mountain like a dog driving a cow, into the barley fields below the county town, in daylight. The tiger-catchers have no choice: forty spears, and the whole town watching. {npc} has to strike first in front of everybody, at something that bites back.

events.text: The man-eater is dead, and with it {npc}'s living. Now {he} has a new plan: a white tiger, the biggest pelt in the province, the bounty of a lifetime. {He} is coming up your mountain with sixty men and a lie for the governor already written. At the shrine at the pass the three ghosts of the north road are still standing, waiting for someone to tell them what happens now.

choices.text: Walk into the governor's hall in human shape with the ledger and the ghosts

effects.log: You recite nine years of lies in front of the governor, and three ghosts stand behind you and nod at the right lines. {npc} is stripped of the captaincy and the bounty is rewritten: paid for man-eaters only, and only with a witness. The old man of the mountain hears it from the magpie and laughs until the coughing starts.

choices.text: Meet the sixty on the mountain and break them, without killing

ok.log: Sixty spears, sixty men thrown into the snow, sixty men who walk home. {npc} walks home last, without a spear, without a hat, without a career. The bounty dies with {his} reputation. The errand is done.

fail.log: You scatter them, but a spear goes in under your shoulder and {npc} gets away with a tuft of white fur and a story. The errand is not done, and now there is a captain who has seen you bleed. (-18 health)

choices.text: Eat {him}

effects.log: The bounty dies with {him}. A new captain is appointed by midsummer, and a ghost in a felt hat walks behind you on the pass, entering your length in a ledger, again and again. The old man of the mountain does not call it done.

events.text: The three ghosts of the north road are still at the shrine, a peddler, a nun and a boy with a bundle of firewood, eaten by a tiger that is dead now, bound to nothing, going nowhere. They look at you the way travellers look at a signpost.

choices.text: Find their families, one by one

effects.log: It takes ten years. The peddler's grandson, the nun's temple, the boy's mother, still alive and ninety. Each one goes home. The boy goes last, and on the threshold turns and waves at you, which ghosts are not supposed to be able to do. (-10 health)

choices.text: Build them a cairn on the bend, with a pot turned over on it

effects.log: Stones, an old steamer pot, an iron spindle through the hole. They go in and settle. It is not home, but it is not the road, and the travellers on the north road cross in ones and twos again.

events.text: The old bear of the north slope is dead, the one who kept the old story of the cave longer than you have been alive. In the cave where she died you find what she left for you: a bundle of mugwort tied with straw, and twenty cloves of wild mountain garlic, still white. Outside, a great birch with its bark peeling stands in the light. Two thousand years ago a tiger sat in a cave like this one and left on the twentieth day, because it was hungry.

choices.text: Go in, and sit with your back to the sun

effects.log: The dark closes behind you like a door. Mugwort is bitter. Garlic is worse. Somewhere above the cave, the birch rustles, and for the first time in your life you count days.

choices.text: Not yet. Eat first, for a month, and then go in

effects.log: You hunt the whole autumn, deer after deer, until the hunger is a small quiet thing in the corner of you. Then you come back to the cave with a full belly and look at the mugwort for a long time.

choices.text: Leave the bundle. A tiger is enough

effects.log: You take one clove of garlic, to remember her by, and do not eat it. The cave stays empty. You are not sure, afterwards, whether that was wisdom or the twentieth day again.

events.text: The cave again, the mugwort, the twenty cloves. Your belly is quiet; you made sure of it. You lie down in the dark where the sun will not reach and begin the count.

choices.text: Begin

effects.log: One day. Two. The dark has a texture, like fur. You eat one leaf of mugwort a day, and it is the worst thing you have ever put in your mouth, including a magistrate.

choices.text: Turn back at the mouth

effects.log: Your paws will not go in. The birch rustles. Next year, perhaps.

events.text: The nineteenth day. The garlic is gone. The mugwort is bitter dust. The hunger has come back, not as a feeling but as a voice, very reasonable, in the exact tone of your grandmother: a deer is grazing at the cave mouth, in the sun. Tomorrow is the twentieth day. Your ancestor sat exactly here, and stood up, and walked out into the light.

choices.text: Stay. Lie on your own paws until the deer is gone

ok.log: The deer grazes all afternoon. You lie on your own forepaws so hard they go numb. At dusk it wanders off. It is the twentieth day, and you are still in the cave, and two thousand years of tigers turn over in their sleep.

fail.log: You are out in the sun with the deer in your jaws before you know you have moved. It is the twentieth day. Of course it is. You sit on the slope eating, and the birch rustles, and the cave mouth behind you is just a hole in a hill.

choices.text: Talk to the hunger, out loud, all night

effects.log: You tell it about the mother on the pass, the ghosts, the magistrate, the cub that was not careful. It listens. By morning it is tired, and so are you, and it is the twentieth day, and you are still here.

choices.text: Go out. You are a tiger

effects.log: The sun is very bright. The deer is very good. Somewhere, a bear laughs, or it is only the birch.

events.text: The twenty-first day. Three sevens. On this day, the old books say, the bear walked out of the cave a woman, and went and sat under the divine birch and prayed for a child. Nothing happens to you. Your paws are still paws. A thin bar of sunlight lies across the cave mouth, exactly where it lay yesterday, like a line drawn on the floor.

choices.text: Do not look at the light. Stay to the hundredth day, as the god asked

effects.log: The bear needed three sevens. The god asked for a hundred. You were always going to need the whole hundred. You put your back to the light and go on counting.

choices.text: Put one paw into the light, to see

effects.log: For one breath, in the bar of sunlight, the paw is a hand: long, brown, with a scar across the knuckles. Then it is a paw again, and you pull it back into the dark as if burnt.

choices.text: Leave now. Twenty-one days is more than any tiger ever did

effects.log: You walk out on four legs, prouder than your ancestor and exactly as much a tiger. The magpie, which had been waiting outside all this time, says that is something, and means it, and also laughs.

events.text: The sixtieth day, or the sixty-first; you have started to lose count, which the god must have expected. Voices at the cave mouth. Tiger-catchers: {npc} and three others, who saw tracks going in and none coming out. "Starved in there," one says. "Or sick. Either way, it is the biggest pelt in the province, and it is not moving." {npc} lights a torch.

choices.text: Do not move. Do not go into the light

ok.log: The torch comes in. It finds a heap of something white in the dark, and {npc} stops, and looks for a long time, and sees, or thinks {he} sees, a person asleep. {He} backs out and tells the others there is nothing in there but an old woman's bundle. Nobody believes {him}, but nobody goes in.

fail.log: A spear comes into the dark and finds your shoulder. You do not move. You do not move. The hunters argue and leave, and you bleed on the cave floor and keep counting.
fail.deathCause: a tiger-catcher's spear in the dark of the cave, on the sixtieth day

choices.text: Go out and drive them off, and come back in

effects.log: Four men run down the mountain. When you turn back to the cave the bar of sunlight is on your back, and the count is broken. You will have to begin again, if you ever do.

events.text: The hundredth day. You know it is the hundredth because the birch outside has dropped every leaf it had, and because the god said a hundred, and because something in you that has been holding its breath since the founding of the world lets it out. The bar of sunlight at the cave mouth is wide now, a whole doorway of it.

choices.text: Walk out into the sun

effects.log: You walk out on two legs. The light is enormous. Your skin is brown and cold and there is no fur on it at all, and you laugh out loud at the sound of your own voice. You go down the mountain and live one whole human life, from the cave to a quiet grave, remembering everything: every deer, every verdict, the taste of mugwort. Two thousand years late, a tiger finished the hundred days.

choices.text: Stay a tiger. It was enough to know you could

effects.log: You walk out on four legs into the sun. You could have walked out on two. The mountain knows it; the magpie knows it; the old man of the mountain, when you pass his pine, bows to you, a little, for the first time. Some victories are kept, not spent.

events.text: The cave on the north slope is empty, the mugwort long gone to dust. But every spring, now, a few women from the village come up with a bundle of mugwort and leave it at the cave mouth, and nobody can tell you why. It has become a custom. Customs, you have learned, are how humans remember what they cannot explain.

choices.text: Lie in the cave mouth on the first warm day, and let them see you

effects.log: They see a white tiger in the cave mouth, chewing mugwort with a face of great suffering. They laugh so hard they have to sit down. The custom is stronger for it.

choices.text: Leave a clove of garlic on the bundle, from the old store

effects.log: One clove, very old, very white. The woman who finds it plants it, and it grows, and her family has wild garlic at the edge of the yard for two hundred years.

events.text: A clear night over the sorghum, and something comes down out of the sky: a rope, shining, the colour of the moon on water. It hangs to the top of an old tree beside a thatched house, and two children in white climb it, hand over hand, out of reach of something that was chasing them. You know this story. You have known it for seven hundred years, and the clothes it began with.

choices.text: Watch them climb, and do not move

effects.log: They go up and up, and become very small, and are gone among the stars. The rope draws up after them. In the morning, the sun is a little brighter than it was, and the moon is a little kinder. The lie in you is still there. It is just quieter.

choices.text: Ask heaven, under your breath, whether there is a rope for you

effects.log: Nothing. The rope draws up after the children. But the sky has heard you, and the sky, you know, keeps everything.

choices.text: Go and find out what was chasing them

effects.log: Only a tiger, a young striped one, lean and ashamed, standing in a woman's skirt that does not fit. It runs when it sees you. You do not follow. You know what it is.

events.text: The thing you did, long ago, comes back in the shape of a smell: a woman's jacket, rice-cake steam, the oil of her hair on the collar. Or it comes back as the words you said in the council of four, the ones that were not true. Either way the sky above the sorghum field is open tonight, and a voice in it, very fair, very patient, is asking whether you have anything to tell it.

choices.text: Tell it everything, the clothes and the lie and all

effects.log: It takes the whole night. The sky does not interrupt. At dawn it simply closes, the way a ledger closes, and you feel lighter by exactly the weight of a woman's jacket.

choices.text: Tell it you have nothing to say

effects.log: The sky waits a long time. Then it says, "Very well," which is the most frightening thing a sky can say.

events.text: You are tired of waiting for the Western seat. Tired of verdicts and errands and old men under pines. It would be so easy: two children climbed to the sky on a rope, and nobody made them fill a docket. You stand at the top of the old tree beside the thatched house, where they stood, and you look up, and you ask. And the sky, which keeps everything, lets down a rope.

choices.text: Climb

effects.log: It holds for the first hundred hand-spans. It holds for the second. Halfway to the stars you hear it, a soft sound like an old sack tearing. The rope was rotten all along; the sky only waited to see if you would climb it. You fall a long way and land in a field of sorghum, and the sorghum is red to this day, and every child in the land knows why.

choices.text: Look at the rope a long time, and climb down out of the tree

effects.log: The rope hangs there all night, swaying. You can see now where it is frayed, where the strands are brown. At dawn it draws back up, and you are still on the ground, a tiger who did not climb. It is the best thing you have done in a century.

choices.text: Bite the end of it, to test it

effects.log: It comes apart in your teeth like wet straw, and the sky pulls it back up quickly, embarrassed. The magpie, who saw it all, tells the whole mountain. You will never live it down. You will live.

events.text: Harvest in the sorghum fields under the mountain. The stalks are red at the root, as they always are, and the children of the village tell each other why while they cut: the tiger, the rope, the fall. One of them, a sharp little girl, says she does not believe it. "A tiger would know a rotten rope," she says. "Tigers are not stupid."

choices.text: Come out of the field edge and agree with her

effects.log: The children scatter screaming, all except the girl, who stands her ground and says, "See?" She grows up to be the headwoman of the village, and nobody ever sells her anything rotten.

choices.text: Stay in the shade and think about stupid tigers

effects.log: Tigers are not stupid. Tigers are hungry, and proud, and in a hurry. You lie in the shade until the reapers go home, thinking about the difference.

events.text: A woodcutter at the shrine at your pass, on {his} knees, before the plank-painting of the old man and the tiger. {npc} is not praying for wood. "Eldest," {he} says to the painting, in a shaking voice. "My family has told it for twenty generations: our first grandmother bore a child in a tiger year, and it went into the mountain and never came back. That is you. I know it is you. Our mother is dying of hunger in a year of no harvest, and I have nothing."

choices.text: Go along with it. Bring a boar to the house of your family

effects.log: A boar at the gate in the morning, neatly killed. And the next month, a deer. {npc} weeps on the threshold. The old woman inside, propped up on quilts, says only, "Took your time," and eats.

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth: you are no one's child

effects.log: {npc} hears it and nods, very calmly, as if {he} had expected it. "Then you are a stranger who knows what hunger is," {he} says. "That will do." You find you have nothing to answer to that.

choices.text: Frighten {him} off the mountain

effects.log: {npc} goes down the pass at a run. The plank-painting looks at you, with its old man and its tiger, and for once you do not like the look of either of them.

events.text: Twenty years of boars at the gate. The old woman, "the eldest's mother" as the whole village now says it, has grown fat and cheerful and terrible, and on fine evenings the old woman sits in the yard and tells the mountain what the old woman thinks of it: the boar was stringy, the deer was late, the eldest never visits properly. {npc} carries the old woman out on {his} back to do it.

choices.text: Come down at dusk and lie in the yard for the scolding

effects.log: The whole village watches from behind its fences: a white tiger the size of a granary, ears flat, being told off by an old woman with a pipe. When the scolding is finished the old woman pats your nose. "Good," comes the verdict. "Eat something. You look thin."

choices.text: Keep bringing meat, but stay in the trees

effects.log: The old woman knows you are there, and talks louder, so you can hear. On the night of the harvest moon a bowl of rice is left on the wall for you, and you eat it, every grain.

events.text: The old woman is dead: in the night, asleep, after a supper of boar declared the best in twenty years. {npc} is in white hemp. The village carries the old woman up to a grave on the slope under your pine. When they have gone home, you come down and lie on the mound, and the snow begins.

choices.text: Do not eat. Do not get up

effects.log: You lie on the grave the whole winter and do not eat, and do not get up, and in the spring the village finds a white tiger on the mound, asleep for good. For a hundred years afterwards the woodcutters say they see young tigers in the high woods with strips of white hemp round their heads, mourning, and every one of them comes down to the grave on the day the old woman died.

choices.text: Mourn three years, as a child does, and then get up

effects.log: Three years on the mound, in snow and rain. You eat only what {npc} leaves at the foot of it. On the last day you stand, shake the snow off, and go back up into the mountain. {npc}'s grandchildren still put a strip of white cloth on the pine every year, for the eldest.

choices.text: Mourn a season, and go back to the Western Palace's work

effects.log: A season is a long time for a tiger. You leave a boar on the grave for the feast of the dead, every year, for as long as the family lasts.

events.text: There is a tiger on the next mountain. Not a rival: you have had rivals, and you know the smell. A tiger as old as the last dynasty, gold and black, who holds the next mountain the way you hold yours, and who, every evening this autumn, has been sitting on the far ridge facing your ridge, not hunting, not marking, just there. They have not crossed the valley. Neither have you.

choices.text: Cross the valley

effects.log: You cross at dusk. They do not get up. You sit down beside them on their ridge and look back at yours, which you have never seen from the outside. It looks smaller than you thought, and lovelier.

choices.text: Sit on your own ridge, facing theirs, every evening

effects.log: A whole autumn of evenings, two tigers on two ridges, facing each other across a valley of red maples. The villagers in between think it is an omen. They are right.

choices.text: You belong to the sky. Look away

effects.log: You look away. The far ridge is empty the next evening, and the next. You tell yourself that is better.

events.text: A year of crossing the valley. You hunt together in the oak woods on their mountain, you lie on the saddle between the two mountains in the long autumn light, and they say, one evening, with their chin on your shoulder: "You keep looking up. At the west. Will you go?"

choices.text: "I do not know"

effects.log: "Good," they say. "Then I will not ask again until you do." They do not ask again for years, and you love them for it.

choices.text: "Yes. One day"

effects.log: They are quiet a long time. "Then I will hold your mountain when you go," they say. "Somebody should."

choices.text: "Not if you ask me to stay"

effects.log: "I will not ask," they say. "But I will not stop you if you decide." It is the most generous thing anyone has ever said to you.

events.text: A morning of perfect autumn sun, not a cloud from horizon to horizon, and it begins to rain: fine, bright, warm rain, every drop lit like a bead. Down in the village the children run out shouting the old words: a tiger is being wed today! On the next mountain, at the edge of the trees, a gold and black tiger is standing in the sun-rain, waiting to see if you will come.

choices.text: Go to them, and give up the sky

effects.log: You go down through the bright rain and up the next mountain, and you do not go back. The Western seat stays empty a while longer. Your line holds both mountains for a thousand years, white cubs and gold, and every time rain falls from a clear sky, the old people of the valley look up at the ridges and smile and say: the tigers are having their anniversary.

choices.text: Go to them, wed in the sun-rain, and keep the sky as well

ok.log: You are wed in the sun-rain on the saddle between the mountains. They know you will go west one day. They say so, in front of the magpie, as a vow. "Until then, both mountains," they say. The rain stops at noon, exactly.

fail.log: You go, and you try to explain about the west, and it comes out wrong, and they turn away into the trees. The rain stops. It is a long winter.

choices.text: Stay on your ridge and watch the rain

effects.log: The rain stops. The far ridge is empty. The children in the village decide the tiger's wedding was called off, and make up a sad song about it, which is still sung.

events.text: Your mate is old now, older than tigers are. They have stopped crossing the valley; you cross it for them. This morning, rain from a clear sky, and they lift their grey muzzle to it and laugh. "Our day," they say. "You always forget."

choices.text: Lie down beside them in the rain until it stops

effects.log: It rains on and off in bright sun all day. They sleep through most of it with their head on your paws. In the spring they do not wake, and you bury them on the saddle between the two mountains, and the sun-rain falls on the grave every year, on the day.

choices.text: Promise them their cubs will hold both mountains

effects.log: They hold you to it. So do the cubs, who are seven hundred years from being anything but foolish, and who chew the magpie's tail at every opportunity.

events.text: The old man of the mountain is very tired. He sits under the pine with his staff across his knees, and the two attendant children who fan him have fallen asleep in the needles. "Eleven hundred years," he says. "You have carried my errands for six hundred of them. A god cannot keep a tiger like you on a mountain for ever. Either I let you go west, or I choose an heir and go where old gods go. I have not decided. Help me."
events.arc: The Old Man Lets You Go

choices.text: "Let me go west, and choose another heir"

effects.log: He looks at you a long time. "Yes," he says. "That is what I would say, in your place. Let us see who else this mountain has." The magpie flies off at once, as if it has been waiting a century for this errand.

choices.text: "Do not go anywhere. I will stay"

effects.log: "You will not," he says, quite kindly. "But I thank you for saying it." He puts a hand on your head, as he did the first day, and leaves it there until the children wake.

choices.text: Ask what the staff weighs

effects.log: "Every grave on the mountain," he says. "Every shrine, every bowl of clean water on every altar, every woodcutter who comes home. It is not heavy. It is only never put down."

events.text: The magpie brings candidates. A young tigress from the east valley, clever and too proud. A bear of the north slope, the granddaughter of the one who told you about the cave. A human: {npc}, a hermit who has swept the mountain shrine for forty years and talks to the plank-painting as if it might answer. The old man looks at all three, and then at you.
events.arc: The Old Man Lets You Go

choices.text: Name the hermit

effects.log: "A human," says the old man, delighted. "The first mountain gods were human. Everybody forgets." {npc} is told, and does not believe it, and goes on sweeping, which is exactly why it is the right choice.

choices.text: Name the young tigress, and promise to teach the young one

effects.log: The tigress is too proud. So were you. You spend twenty years teaching the young tigress that a god's tiger carries children, and twenty more that a god does too. The lesson takes, slowly, and costs you only two bites.

choices.text: Name none of them. Take the staff yourself

effects.log: The old man is silent. Then comes a laugh, and the staff is held out to you. "I wondered," says the god, "whether you would say it."

events.text: The old man stands up for the first time in a century, slowly, with a hand on your shoulder. He is holding out his staff, gnarled pine, polished by a thousand years of his hand. "Take it," he says, "and every shrine painting from now on is of an old man and a tiger, and both are you. Or do not, and go west, and I will find another hand."
events.arc: The Old Man Lets You Go

choices.text: Take the staff

effects.log: The staff is light. It is only never put down. You feel the mountain go into you, every grave, every spring, every bowl of clean water, and you sit down under the pine as an old man with a white beard and a white tiger at your feet, and both of them are you. The old god walks away down the ridge into the mist, whistling, and is not seen again.

choices.text: Close his hand back round it. Go west

effects.log: "Then go," says the old man of the mountain, and takes his hand off your shoulder for the last time. "You are released, my tiger. All my errands are done." He sits back down under the pine, and is asleep before you reach the ridge.

events.text: The heir is ready, or ready enough. The old man of the mountain calls you to the pine on the autumn equinox, with the magpie and the two sleepy children and the whole mountain listening. "Your errands are done," he says, "all six of them. I have no more to give you. Go west, my tiger. You are released."
events.arc: The Old Man Lets You Go

choices.text: Bow to the ground

effects.log: You put your great head down on the needles at his feet. He puts his hand on it, as he did the first day, six hundred years ago. When you lift your head the pine is empty, and the staff is leaning against it, waiting for the heir.

choices.text: Ask for one more errand, the last

effects.log: "Very well," he says. "Come back once every hundred years and see that the shrine water is clean." It is the only errand he ever gave you that was for himself, and you never once miss it.

events.text: The heir has been on the mountain a hundred years. The shrine painting has changed: the old man in it has a different face now, and the tiger at the god's feet is a different tiger. Woodcutters still bow to it at the pass. The water on the altar is clean. You came back to see that it was.
events.arc: The Old Man Lets You Go

choices.text: Drink from the altar bowl, as you used to

effects.log: The new god sees, and laughs, and fills the bowl again. "He said you would," says the god. "He said you always did."

choices.text: Sit in the shrine painting's place for an afternoon

effects.log: A woodcutter comes round the bend, sees a white tiger sitting where the painting is, looks at the painting, looks at you, and sits down on the road and laughs until he cries.

events.text: A dream comes down from the north with news: a king of the north is dying, and a painter has been working for a year in a granite chamber under a mound, painting the four walls. The north wall has its tortoise, the south its bird, the east its dragon. On the west wall the painter has stopped, brush in hand, for three months. "I cannot make it right," {npc} tells the lamp. "I have never seen one."

choices.text: Go north, and stand in the lamplight

effects.log: {npc} looks up from the lamp and sees you in the doorway of the tomb: white, star-barred, and on your shoulders the new orange wings, half-folded. The brush falls. {He} picks it up again with a hand that shakes, and begins.

choices.text: Send the painter a dream instead

effects.log: That night {npc} dreams of a tiger with a neck as long as a heron's, mouth wide, wings like autumn maples. In the morning {he} paints it before breakfast, and it is better than any tiger that ever lived, and not quite you.

choices.text: A tomb is no place for a tiger. Stay west

effects.log: The painter finishes the west wall from an old pattern-book. It is a perfectly good tiger. Nobody in the tomb will complain.

events.text: {npc} paints for nine days without sleeping, in lime-white and ochre and the red that comes from the hills: your neck stretched long, your mouth wide open, the wings orange as maple leaves. On the ninth night {he} puts down the brush and sits back against the north wall, under the tortoise. "The king will die in the spring," {he} says. "The king is afraid of the dark. Will the tiger keep the west for the king?"

choices.text: "For a while"

effects.log: {npc} nods, satisfied. "A while is longer than a king," {he} says, and puts out the lamp, and sleeps for two days in the tomb with the four guardians watching.

choices.text: "Paint the eyes open, and I will"

effects.log: {He} paints the eyes open, and when the last stroke is dry, the tiger on the west wall looks out at the dark, and so, a little, do you, from very far away.

choices.text: "No. I am going to the sky"

effects.log: {npc} is quiet. "Then it is a painting," {he} says, "and paintings fade." {He} puts out the lamp, and you are both in the dark, and neither of you likes it.

events.text: The king of the north is buried. The stone door is sliding shut on the chamber, and inside, in the last of the torchlight, four guardians stand on four walls round a sleeper who was afraid of the dark. The west wall is yours. You could step into it. The painting would hold you; it was made to. You would keep one sleeper for a thousand years, while the white flaked away.

choices.text: Step into the west wall

effects.log: You step into the lime and the ochre, and the stone door closes, and it is dark, and you are not afraid. Thirteen centuries. The king's bones go to dust. The white of your coat flakes off the granite grain by grain, until only the long neck, the open mouth and the orange wings are left, still bright. One day, a long time later, a lamp comes in, and someone gasps, and you are still there.

choices.text: Leave a little of yourself in the paint, and go

effects.log: You breathe once on the wet wall. Something of you goes into it, enough to keep a frightened king company. The door closes. You go back west, and once every few hundred years you feel the dark of that tomb like an itch under one wing.

choices.text: Go, and let the painting be a painting

effects.log: The door closes on a good painting. Paintings fade. Kings are not, as far as you can tell, afraid of anything once they are dead.

events.text: Three hundred years later, a far-off itch under one wing: grave robbers in the tomb of the north. They have dug through the mound and are prying at the stone door with iron bars. Inside, the four guardians are only paint.

choices.text: Wake the tiger on the west wall

effects.log: The robbers get the door open, lift their lamp, and see, on the west wall, a white tiger with its mouth wide open turn its long neck and look at them. They are found a week later in the next county, still running.

choices.text: Let the earth fall in over the door

effects.log: A small landslide, very precise. The door is buried again under the mound, and the robbers dig somewhere else, and the king sleeps on.

events.text: Four hundred tiger-catchers, the whole of the king's corps, led by {npc}: the greatest captain they have ever had, tested with the bow and the spear and the stone, who has struck first on forty tigers and counts every one. The court wants a white pelt for the throne dais, to prove the reign is blessed. The corps comes up your mountain in four columns, with dogs, beaters, gongs and a drum.

choices.text: Go to ground in the high crags

ok.log: Three weeks in a crack in the crags while the corps combs the mountain below. The dogs lose you. {npc} does not. On the last day {he} stands under your crag and looks up, straight at you, and then gives the order to go home.

fail.log: The dogs find you on the second day. You go out through the line in a storm of spears and leave blood on the snow for a mile. (-20 health)

choices.text: Lead them across three mountains, and lose them

effects.log: A month of it. Four hundred men, three mountains, one tiger. By the end the corps is in tatters and you are thin as a fox, and {npc} has your measure exactly. (-10 health)

choices.text: Walk out onto the summit and let them see you

effects.log: Four hundred men stop climbing. The drum stops. A white tiger made of stars on a summit in the snow. Some of the beaters kneel. {npc} does not. {He} takes out a whetstone and begins to sharpen a spear.

events.text: {npc} has done the sums. The corps has burned the village under your pass, not the houses, only the barns, and taken its people into the county town. A message is nailed to the shrine at the pass: they will be released the day the white tiger comes down. {npc} wrote it out by hand, plainly, without threats. {He} does not need any.

choices.text: Go into the county town at night in human shape and free them

ok.log: A grey traveller talks to the guards about the weather until they sleep, and the prison is empty by dawn. {npc}, when {he} finds out, laughs once, and orders the corps back up the mountain.

fail.log: The guard is awake, and {npc} knows a tiger's walk under any face. You get out over the wall with a spear-cut and nothing else. (-15 health)

choices.text: Roar from the pass until the whole county hears

effects.log: The roar goes down the valley like a landslide, and the county town shuts its gates. The villagers stay prisoners. {npc} hears the roar and writes it down: one more thing {he} knows about you.

events.text: The last day of the hunt. {npc} has you in a high valley with a cliff behind, four hundred spears in front, and the villagers of the pass, the ones who leave meat at your shrine, standing in a line before the corps, roped, as a shield. {He} walks forward alone. "Come down," {he} says. "Come down and they go home. You know I will not lie to you. I never have."

choices.text: Come down

effects.log: You come down off the cliff and walk through the four hundred and lie down in front of {npc}, and {he} keeps {his} word: the villagers go home. {He} strikes first. The white pelt goes on the throne dais, to prove a reign was blessed. For centuries afterwards the pelt changes hands for a fortune, and nobody who owns it is ever lucky again.

choices.text: The Tiger Comes Down: break the line, take none of the roped

ok.log: You come down the cliff like a falling star and go through the line of spears and not one roped villager is touched. When it is over the corps is running and {npc} is on {his} back in the snow with your paw on {his} chest. You let {him} up. {He} never hunts again.

fail.log: Four hundred spears is four hundred spears. You break the line and get out over the ridge, and leave a great deal of yourself in the snow.
fail.deathCause: the four hundred spears of the tiger-catching corps, in the high valley

choices.text: Call the magpie and the mountain god, and wait

ok.log: A snowstorm comes down on the high valley out of a clear sky, so thick that four hundred men cannot see their own spears. When it lifts, the villagers have been untied by someone very old with a white beard, and you are gone.

fail.log: Nothing comes. The old man of the mountain is tired, or asleep, or busy. You go out over the cliff the hard way. (-20 health)

events.text: Winter again, and the snow writes every step you take. Every county has sent its tiger-catchers, and they have stopped beating the slopes for anything that moves: they are following one track, yours, and the bounty on it has been doubled twice. From the ridge you can count their fires. Tonight there is a line of them across the only way out of the valley.

choices.text: Go to ground in the winter den, and let the snow close over your track

effects.log: You lie in the den with your nose under your tail while the snow writes over everything. Nine days. The fires go out one by one, and the catchers go home to argue about whose tiger you were. You come out thin and unseen. (-4 health)

choices.text: Break the line at night: The Tiger Comes Down

ok.log: You come down the slope into the fires and out the other side before the first gong. Behind you a line of spears points at an empty valley, and the bounty is never posted again in that county.

fail.log: There are more of them than the fires said. You break through with spear-cuts down both flanks and a long night of running, and the bounty is doubled again. (-30 health)
fail.deathCause: the spears of the tiger-catchers on the ridge

choices.text: Stop running. Lie down on the ridge and let them come

effects.log: You lie down on the ridge where the snow is deepest and watch them come up the slope with their torches. The first spear is a gift, from the captain who counts. The pelt goes to the capital, to prove a reign was blessed, and the mountain is very quiet for a hundred years.

events.text: {npc} is old and does not hunt. {He} has come up the mountain alone, without a spear, to the shrine at the pass, and is sitting in front of the plank-painting with a jar of water and two cups. "I counted forty tigers," {he} says to the painting. "I never counted the one I did not take. I think I would like to."

choices.text: Sit down across from {him}

effects.npcPass: old age, an old hunter who stopped counting
effects.log: You sit. {npc} pours two cups of water, drinks one, and leaves the other in front of you. You talk until dark, an old hunter and an old tiger, about weather and dogs and the mountains that are gone. {He} dies that winter. The cup is still on the shrine.

choices.text: Let {him} see you from the trees, and go

effects.npcPass: old age, an old hunter who stopped counting
effects.log: {He} sees, and nods, and finishes the water. That night the county records that the captain of the corps was buried with an empty quiver, at {his} own request.

events.text: Under the three straight stars of the Balance, three small ones, low and cold and red: the Punishment. You have never noticed how close they are to you until tonight. They are calling. Not with words. With the sound a sword makes coming out of a scabbard, very slowly, all night.

choices.text: Listen

effects.log: They tell you what you are: just, very often. They have watched every verdict, and they approve. They are the only part of the sky that does.

choices.text: Go down to the valley and pardon the first person you meet

effects.log: A chicken thief, terrified. You let him go with the chicken. The red stars dim a little. The magpie, on the pine, says it is a start.

events.text: Every execution in the land, this autumn, you feel: the dry day after the equinox, the square, the sword, the crowd. Some of them were guilty. You know which. A herald stands in your path on the ridge at dawn, human-faced, with a tiger's paws and an axe across its shoulder, and bows. "The Punishment has no keeper," it says. "It has been waiting for one who is never merciful. The seat is under the belt. Come."

choices.text: Go with the herald

effects.log: You walk up the axe-light into the west and lie down under the three straight stars, and become the three small red ones. Every execution in the land falls under you after that, every one, for ever. You are just, very often. You are merciful, never. You are alone, always, and in time you stop noticing.

choices.text: Refuse. Sit in the Autumn Court and pardon all year

effects.log: The herald shoulders its axe and waits on the ridge for a year while you pardon a thief, a deserter, a widow, a bandit who did not deserve it. At the end of the year it bows and goes. The red stars are dim. The beam has begun, very slowly, to come up.

choices.text: Ask the herald who kept the Punishment before

effects.log: "Nobody," says the herald. "Nobody has ever been severe enough. You are the first who came close." It sounds sorry for you. That is worse than anything else it could have said.

events.text: The red stars under the belt are quiet now, dimmer than you have ever seen them. Below the pass, in the autumn court, a boy accused of theft stands in front of you, shaking. He did it. You know he did it. He is eleven.

choices.text: Pardon him, and give him a deer for his family

effects.log: He runs home with a deer over his shoulders that is bigger than he is. The magpie, for the first time in a century, lands on your head and does not laugh.

choices.text: A small punishment, fairly given

effects.log: He sweeps the shrine at the pass for a season. He grows up to sweep it for years, by choice, and tells everyone the white tiger was the only fair judge he ever met.

events.text: New Year, and the folk painters are out on the pass again with their brushes, as they always are, sketching the tiger for the magpie-and-tiger pictures people hang on their gates. Only this year they are not afraid of you at all. One of them walks right up and pats your head to see if it is soft. The magpie sits down on it and laughs.

choices.text: Laugh with them

effects.log: You laugh. They draw you laughing, with your eyes round and your teeth like a row of rice cakes. The picture sells in every market in the province. The bandits buy three.

choices.text: Roar, once, for the first time in years

effects.log: They drop their brushes and run. The magpie stays on your head, but it stops laughing, and looks down at you with interest.

events.text: Bandits hold the pass now, the gang you kept pardoning. A man-eater from the north, one more you let go because it said it was sorry, walks your lower slopes. The villagers have stopped leaving meat at the shrine. They leave it at the bandits' camp instead. In every gate in the province hangs a painting of a fool tiger with a magpie on its head, and the magpie is real, and it is on your head now.

choices.text: Sit under the pine and let it be so

effects.log: You pardoned everyone. It seemed like kindness every time. The bandits hold the pass for a hundred years, and the man-eater eats, and in every New Year painting from now until the end of painting there is a tiger with round eyes and a stupid grin under a pine, and a magpie on its head, laughing. The children love it. That is the sad part.

choices.text: Go down to the bandits' camp tonight

effects.log: There is no pardon in the camp that night. In the morning the pass is empty, and the man-eater on your lower slopes leaves the mountain without being asked. The magpie flies off your head and sits on the pine where it belongs.

choices.text: Punish the man-eater, and pardon the bandits once more

effects.log: The man-eater is gone by dawn. The bandits watch you come back past their camp with blood on your muzzle, and decide on their own that the pass is not as comfortable as it was.

events.text: A folk painter on the pass at New Year, sketching. The tiger in the sketch is a fool, as they always are, with the magpie on its head. But this painter has drawn the fool tiger with one paw on a bandit's neck, very firmly. "That is the new way," the painter says, without looking up. "Since last year."

choices.text: Pose

effects.log: You hold the paw up for an hour. The magpie on your head poses too. It is the best-selling picture in the province for years.

choices.text: Ask for the fool to be taken out

effects.log: "Then nobody would buy it," says the painter reasonably. "A tiger has to be a little foolish. Otherwise people are afraid to hang it up."

events.text: Your ghosts have started walking in a line. They used to drift behind you, each alone, calling its own name. Now they go ahead of you on the pass at dusk in a row, with lanterns that give no light, and they call together, and the voice they call in is a mother's. Travellers come up from the valley at the sound and do not know why.

choices.text: Stand in the road and turn the travellers back

effects.log: You sit in the road like a fallen tree, and the travellers who come up toward their mothers' voices find a white tiger instead, and run home, and live. The ghosts look back at you over their shoulders. They are not pleased. (-8 health)

choices.text: Let them lead. They are yours

effects.log: A salt peddler comes up the pass to a voice that sounds exactly like his mother. You are waiting at the top. The ghosts have a new companion in the morning, and they are delighted.

choices.text: Lay the first of them to rest, tonight

effects.log: You take the oldest of them by the hand, so to speak, and lead it to a cairn and a pot turned over. The line is one shorter. The others watch you go with their empty lanterns. (-10 health)

events.text: The ghosts have made a kind of court on the pass. They have built it out of nothing, a hall of mist with a seat at the head, and they bow to the seat when you walk by. "Lord," they call you, in their mothers' voices. "Lord of the pass. Sit. We will bring you everyone." The village under the pass has no lights tonight. Nobody has crossed since spring.

choices.text: Sit in the seat

effects.log: You sit. They bring you everyone. For three hundred years nobody crosses the mountain, and the ghosts go on walking ahead of you on the pass at dusk, more every year, calling names in the voices of mothers. The village under the pass is abandoned. Its name is lost. The pass is not: it is the first thing every child in the province is warned about, and the last thing any of them ever sees, if they forget.

choices.text: Break the seat, and lay them to rest one by one, if it takes a century

effects.log: The hall of mist comes apart under your paws. Then the long work: cairns, pots, spindles, families found three provinces away. Two of them go home this year. The others wait in the road, quieter now, watching you, as if they want to see whether you will really do it. (-20 health)

choices.text: Roar them silent

effects.log: The ghosts go quiet for a decade. The village lights one lamp, then two. But they are still there, in the road, waiting, and you know it.

events.text: A shaman comes up the pass alone at dusk, an old woman with a brass bell, a white paper fan and a bundle of five-coloured cloth, the first human to cross in years. She stops among your ghosts and begins to ring the bell. "I have come for them," she says, to the dark where you are lying. "Not for you. You can watch, if you like."

choices.text: Watch, and help her find their names

effects.log: All night she sings them, one by one, and you give her their names when she falters: the peddler, the nun, the salt carrier, the girl with the water jar. Two walk away into the morning with her. She comes back the next year, and the next.

choices.text: Let her work, and guard the pass so nothing troubles her

effects.log: One goes with her. She bows to the dark where you are lying, on her way down. "Next year," she says. "Have the others ready."

events.text: It takes a tortoise eleven years to climb a mountain, and this one has done it without stopping: a black tortoise as big as a threshing floor, a black serpent coiled round its shell, both heads talking at once. The Black Tortoise, guardian of the north. "The council of the four directions," says the tortoise. "Will read your record," says the serpent. "Before the west seat is filled," they finish together. "Bring your docket. Bring your dead."

choices.text: Bow to the north

effects.log: The tortoise approves. The serpent says it has seen better bows, from a dragon, once. They argue about which dragon for the rest of the afternoon, and you understand that this is how the north does everything.

choices.text: Ask what the record is for

effects.log: "Autumn judges every living thing," says the serpent. "So the one who keeps autumn," says the tortoise, "must have been judged first." They seem to find this obvious. At their age, perhaps it is.

choices.text: Tell them a tiger keeps no record but its teeth

effects.log: "Then we will read your teeth," says the tortoise mildly, and the serpent laughs, a dry sound like ice cracking on a river.

events.text: The council terrace, high above the clouds. The Black Tortoise has your docket written on the inside of its shell. It reads it aloud, mansion by mansion: Legs, Bond, Stomach, Hairy Head, Net, Turtle Beak, Three Stars. At each one the serpent looks at you, and asks one question: "Was it just?"

choices.text: Answer for each case, truly, the bare stripes too

effects.log: Some you defend. Some you cannot. The tortoise writes your answers on its shell, and the serpent, at the end, says only: "It knows what it did. That is more than most."

choices.text: Answer that all seven are full and every verdict was just

effects.log: The tortoise checks. The serpent checks. The seven stars on your coat burn, every one. "So it is," says the tortoise. "Seldom," says the serpent, "is it so."

choices.text: Say every verdict was just, even the ones that were not

effects.log: The tortoise writes it down without a word. The serpent looks at you a long time with its flat cold eyes, and then looks away. In the sky, far off, something shifts, like a rope being let out a little.

events.text: The Vermilion Bird comes up from the south in a column of heat, every feather a flame, voice like a temple bell rung by a child. It does not read your record. It sings it. It sings your ghosts: the ones still behind you, one by one, with their names and their villages and the road where you met them. It sings very well. The council listens without moving.

choices.text: Listen to the end, and name each ghost with it

effects.log: You name every one, and the bird sings each name a little softer than the last. When it is done it bows to you, unexpectedly. "You know them," it says. "The ones who eat men usually forget." Then: "Lay them down before you sit."

choices.text: Ask for a century to lay them all to rest first

effects.log: The council grants it. The tortoise says a century is short. The serpent says for a tiger it is long. The bird says nothing, and burns a little warmer.

choices.text: Tell the bird that hunger is not a crime

effects.log: "No," sings the bird. "But they are not hunger. They are people." The ghosts behind you all turn to look at it, and then, slowly, at you.

events.text: The Vermilion Bird comes up from the south in a column of heat, and looks at you sideways out of an eye like a coal. It came to sing your ghosts. There are none. It walks round you twice, sniffing, as a bird can sniff, and lands on the terrace looking almost disappointed. "A tiger with no dead behind it," it says. "Either you never ate, or you laid every one to rest. Which?"

choices.text: "I laid them to rest"

effects.log: The bird sings the cairns instead: the pots turned over, the spindles, the families found in far valleys. It is a much shorter song, and a better one.

choices.text: "I was hungry for a thousand years, and never ate a human"

effects.log: The bird looks at you for a long time. "That," it says, "is a much stranger song." It sings it anyway, to the whole sky, and the north writes it down on its shell.

events.text: The Azure Dragon comes to the council from the east, from the left ridge of the valley you have shared for five hundred years. It walks into the circle, lies down beside you, and says only: "I have shared rain with the tiger on the right ridge for five centuries. It has quarrelled with me, and it was right. It has lain on the saddle through every bad winter beside me. It is worthy. I will speak for it as long as you like."

choices.text: Thank it, in front of everyone

effects.log: "Do not," says the dragon, embarrassed, and looks away east for a long time. The Black Tortoise writes something on its shell. Somewhere in the south, a bird laughs.

choices.text: Tell the council the times the dragon was right and you were wrong

effects.log: There are more than you expected. The dragon lies through all of it with its whiskers flat, and on the way home it walks closer to you than it has in a century.

events.text: The Azure Dragon comes to the council from the east, and does not look at you. It lays a slab of birch bark on the terrace: a list, in claw marks, of every traveller who vanished on the right ridge in five hundred years, every quarrel over the rain, every dry spring you blamed on it. "The west wants a guardian," it tells the council. "Fine. Let the tiger say what it did for the valley between us."

choices.text: Answer for each line on the bark

effects.log: It takes a month. Some lines you defend. Some you cannot. At the end the dragon takes back its bark and looks at it and says, quietly, "Fewer than I thought." That is a beginning.

choices.text: Roar the dragon down

effects.log: The terrace shakes. The dragon does not move a scale. "Thank you," it says. "That was my last line."

choices.text: Offer the dragon the next ten springs of rain, first

effects.log: The dragon blinks. It had expected an argument. "Five," it says at last. "Five is enough. I will not have it said the east was greedy." Ten springs later, on the saddle between the ridges, it lies down beside you for the first time.

events.text: A witness is called: {npc}, a human of the upper heavens, who tells the council that long ago, before {he} ever climbed to the clouds, {he} stood as a child in a maple clearing in white clothes while a white tiger on a flat rock judged the quarrel of two villages. "I was frightened," {npc} says. "I was also listened to. I want the council to know how the tiger listened."

choices.text: Let {him} tell it

effects.log: {npc} tells it well: the maple clearing, the flat rock, the magpie on its branch writing, the long minute the tiger gave to each side before it spoke. The Black Tortoise writes the whole of it on the inside of its shell, and runs out of room.

choices.text: Ask {him} whether you judged rightly

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it in front of the four directions for a long time. "Yes," {he} says at last. "And when you were not sure, you said so." The serpent nods, as if that were the only thing that mattered.

events.text: The Yellow Dragon of the centre, of earth and of the late summer between all seasons, has been silent through the whole of the council. Now it lifts its head and looks at the three straight stars in your coat, the Balance, and weighs them, the way a farmer weighs a sack of grain in two hands. "You lean," it says. "Toward mercy. Autumn that never cuts does not harvest. Why should the west be given to you?"

choices.text: "Because I can learn to cut"

effects.log: "Then learn," says the centre. "We will wait." It does, with the patience of farmland. Every verdict you give that autumn has a little more iron in it.

choices.text: "Because mercy was always the harder verdict"

ok.log: The Yellow Dragon considers it for a whole night. "True," it says in the morning. "And still not enough." But it sounds less certain than it did.

fail.log: The centre does not argue. It only goes on looking at you, with the patience of farmland, until you look away.

events.text: The Yellow Dragon of the centre lifts its head and weighs the three straight stars in your coat, the Balance, like a farmer weighing a sack of grain. "You lean," it says. "Toward the Punishment. Autumn that only cuts leaves nothing for the spring. The east would have to plant in ashes. Why should the west be given to you?"

choices.text: "Because I can learn to spare"

effects.log: "Then learn," says the centre, and settles to wait, with the patience of farmland. That autumn you pardon a deserter, a poacher and a thief, and none of them come back.

choices.text: "Because someone must be severe, and the others will not"

effects.log: The Yellow Dragon is silent for so long the stars move. "The Punishment star," it says at last, "has been empty since the world began. Be careful it does not fit you."

events.text: The Yellow Dragon of the centre weighs the three straight stars of the Balance in your coat, and finds them level. It weighs them again, to be sure. "Level," it says, and for the first time in the council it sounds pleased. "The beam held level by a predator. I have seen kings who could not do it. Tell me how."

choices.text: "I was afraid of both ends"

effects.log: "Good," says the Yellow Dragon. "The ones who fear neither fall off one." The tortoise writes it down. The bird sings one note. Even the serpent nods.

choices.text: "My grandmother told me a tiger who never forgives is a trap, and a tiger who always forgives is a rug"

effects.log: The Vermilion Bird laughs so hard it sets fire to the tortoise's record, and the serpent has to put it out, and the council adjourns for a day. The Yellow Dragon, before it goes, repeats the saying quietly to itself, twice, as if storing it.

events.text: You take your place in the west of the council, and for the first time the circle is closed: the black north, the burning south, the azure east, the white west, and the gold of the centre that has no direction because it is all of them. "The record is read," says the Yellow Dragon. "Now tell me what you will do with autumn."

choices.text: "Harvest. And judge only what must be judged"

effects.log: "Then do," says the Yellow Dragon, as if that settles everything, and it does. The north writes it on the shell. The south sings one note. In the east, the dragon lets out a breath it has held for five hundred years.

choices.text: "Hold the beam level, every year, for ever"

effects.log: "For ever is a long time to stand still," says the Yellow Dragon. "Good. That is what the centre does, too." It sounds, for a moment, almost lonely, and then not.

choices.text: "I do not know yet. I will learn it from the orchards"

effects.log: "Good," says the Yellow Dragon. "The ones who know already are the ones we have to replace." The council does not end. It simply begins, and you are part of it.

events.text: A quarrel in the council. The south wants a long hot summer for the rice; the north wants a hard early frost to kill the locust eggs; the east wants a wet spring. And the west, which is you, has been asked to bring an autumn that will satisfy all of them. The Yellow Dragon in the middle has declined to have an opinion and is pretending to sleep.

choices.text: Bring autumn late, so the rice can finish, and then hard

effects.log: The rice finishes. The frost comes the next week, all at once, and every locust egg in the land dies. The north is satisfied, the south nearly is, and nobody can prove whose idea it was.

choices.text: Let the dragon and the bird fight it out, and watch

effects.log: The fight is spectacular and lasts a week. The weather that year is very strange. Every guardian learns something about the others, and the Yellow Dragon, who was not asleep at all, writes it down.

choices.text: Decide. You are the autumn

effects.log: Autumn comes on the day you say. Nobody argues. Afterwards you notice that nobody argues with you any more about anything, and you are not sure that is good.

events.text: An envoy of the Jade court arrives at the council terrace with a retinue of clerks and a mandate to audit the four guardians: winds, rains, harvests, verdicts, every century accounted for. The tortoise produces its shell. The bird produces a song. The envoy turns to the west.

choices.text: Produce a dead deer

effects.log: You lay it at the envoy's feet, a fine red deer, freshly killed. The clerks stop writing. The envoy looks at the deer, then at you, then at the deer. "That is not what was asked for," it says. "It is what the west has," you say. The Black Tortoise laughs out loud with both heads.

choices.text: Recite every verdict of the Autumn Court, by year

ok.log: It takes nine days. You do not miss a case. The clerks run out of ink twice. At the end the envoy closes the ledger and says, "The west is in order," and the dragon in the east, unaccountably, looks proud of you.

fail.log: You lose count somewhere in the fourth century and the envoy notes it, kindly, in red. The bird does not let you forget it for an age.

choices.text: Show the envoy the orchards in autumn

effects.log: You take it down from the stars and walk it through a hundred valleys at harvest: persimmons strung under the eaves, red peppers drying on the roofs, rice in stooks. The envoy stops writing halfway through and simply looks.

events.text: The audit continues for a decade. The envoy wants to know about the ghosts: how many were made, how many laid to rest, where the cairns are. The clerks have a separate ledger for it, bound in white hemp, and they handle it as if it were cold.

choices.text: Take the envoy to every cairn

effects.log: Up every pass you ever kept. At each cairn the envoy stops and reads the name, if there is one, and writes it. At the last one, an old pot on a pile of stones on the north road, the envoy stands for a long time without writing anything at all. (-8 health)

choices.text: Tell the envoy the ledger is in the bird's song

effects.log: The envoy sends for the bird. The bird is delighted. The audit of the ghosts takes three years and is, the clerks agree, the most beautiful audit in the history of the Jade court.

events.text: The audit is concluded. The envoy is packing its ledgers. It has written one more line, at the bottom of the west's page, and it shows you before it closes the book: Deer, one. Received.

choices.text: Ask who audits the Jade court

effects.log: The envoy goes very still. The clerks stop packing. The Black Tortoise, to everyone's surprise, laughs again with both heads. The envoy leaves an hour early.

choices.text: Give the envoy another deer, for the road

effects.log: The envoy accepts it, with the expression of someone who will be asked about it for a thousand years. It is entered in the ledger. Deer, two.

events.text: Two hundred years later, a new envoy, a new audit. This one has read the old ledger first. It stands on the council terrace, looks at you, and says carefully: "I have been told to ask the west not to bring a deer."

choices.text: Bring a boar

effects.log: The envoy writes it down with a perfectly straight face. Boar, one. The tortoise laughs so hard it has to be helped back onto its feet by the serpent.

choices.text: Bring the audit itself: every verdict since the last

effects.log: The new envoy is almost disappointed. It reads your record for a year and finds it in order, and goes home, and tells everyone the west has grown dull. You do not mind.

events.text: The valley between the ridges is holding a festival: a thousand years since the first family built where the water winds. They have the flat stone where the first bowl of rice was left, and a family that still claims the first house. On the left ridge, the Azure Dragon is lying in the pines with its chin on the saddle, watching the lanterns. On the right ridge, you are doing the same.

choices.text: Cross the saddle and lie down beside it

effects.log: The dragon moves over without a word. The whole valley looks up and sees both ridges at once in the lantern light, and for a moment the noise of the festival stops.

choices.text: Send the valley a good harvest, in the dragon's name

effects.log: The granaries are full that year. The valley thanks the dragon. The dragon, who knows better, sends a deer over the saddle the next morning, which is how the east says thank you to the west.

choices.text: Watch from your own ridge, and count the roofs

effects.log: Six hundred and twelve. You remember when there was one, and you were lying here, and the left ridge was empty.

events.text: A winter night on the saddle between the ridges, snow on both your backs. The dragon talks, for once. "They are calling you west," it says. "And they are calling me east. And this valley has never known a bad year since we both lay down. I have been wondering what happens to it when we go."

choices.text: "It will learn to have bad years, like everyone"

effects.log: "Yes," says the dragon. "I suppose that is fair." Neither of you sounds convinced. The snow goes on falling.

choices.text: "Perhaps we do not go"

effects.log: The dragon is silent for a long time. Then it puts its great head down on the saddle beside yours. "Perhaps," it says.

events.text: The autumn equinox. The Western Palace is lit above you, seven mansions, and the way to it is open, or nearly. Below, the valley is gold to the rims. On the saddle between the ridges, the Azure Dragon has come out of the pines and lain down, and is watching you, and waiting.

choices.text: Lie down with the dragon, right ridge and left, for ever

effects.log: You go down to the saddle and lie beside the dragon, and neither of you gets up again. Right ridge and left ridge, white and azure, you hold the valley between you like two hands around a bowl, and the people at its heart never know a bad year, and argue for a thousand years about which ridge is the lucky one.

choices.text: Not yet. The west is still open

effects.log: You go up into the equinox and come down again, as you always have. The dragon yawns enormously and goes back into its pines. There will be other autumns.

choices.text: Go and lie down on your own ridge, and think
