effects.log: You lie on the right ridge all night. The dragon lies on the saddle. Neither of you says anything, and the valley sleeps between you, not knowing it is being decided about.

events.text: Spring, and the dragon comes over the saddle dripping wet with a bundle of something in its jaws, which it drops at your feet: a cub, white, barred, soaked, furious. Yours, or your line's, many generations down, fallen into the dragon's stream again. "It is the same one," says the dragon. "Every three hundred years. Your family has a talent."

choices.text: Teach it to swim, finally

effects.log: It takes a summer. By the end the cub can swim like an otter and has a terrible habit of riding on the dragon's head. The dragon says nothing about it, which, you are fairly sure, means it is delighted.

choices.text: Shake the cub dry and send it home

effects.log: It goes home, sneezing. The dragon watches it go. "Spoiled," it says. "But alive." It sounds pleased.

events.text: A great gut on the hill above the valley at harvest: a mudang in layered robes of the five colours, two drummers, a cymbal player, and five long flags on bamboo poles, blue, red, white, black and yellow. The mudang turns to each direction in turn and calls its emperor down: the Blue Emperor of the east, the Red Emperor of the south, the Black Emperor of the north, the Yellow Emperor of the centre. Then the mudang spins west, with a white fan and a bell, and stops dead, facing you.

choices.text: Come down into the white flag

effects.log: The white silk fills like a sail on a windless evening, and the mudang staggers, laughing, and the drummers lose the beat. Every persimmon on the hillside goes orange at once. The village will talk about nothing else until the snow.

choices.text: Come as the cold west wind only, and let the rite go on

effects.log: A clean cold wind runs once round the hill, through the white flag and away, and every leaf on the hill lets go together. The mudang feels it and finishes the rite as if nothing happened, which is how the best of them do it.

choices.text: You are a tiger, not an emperor. Stay on the ridge

effects.log: The mudang calls three times, then smiling moves on to the next part of the rite. The white flag hangs still. Autumn comes anyway, a week late, and nobody minds.

events.text: After the rite the mudang lets the village pick its fortune from the five flags, rolled tight on their poles: pull one blind, and the colour tells the year. A small child, {npc}, has pulled the white flag five autumns running, and the mudang has started to look up at the west thoughtfully while {he} does it.

choices.text: Let {him} pull white again

mem.note: gave me the white flag every year

effects.log: Six autumns. Then seven. When {npc} is grown, the mudang takes the child of the white flag as an apprentice, and the valley has a mudang of its own who never once has to call the west twice.

choices.text: Let {him} pull red this year, so the world does not seem arranged for one child

effects.log: Red: a hot, hard year. {npc} cries, then works harder than anyone in the valley all summer, and pulls white again the next autumn, and is much less surprised about it.

events.text: A herald comes to you on the ridge, the one the old books describe and no one has seen: human-faced, tiger-pawed, an axe of white metal across its shoulder. The herald of autumn. It kneels, which you did not know heralds did. "The White Emperor's seat has had no one in it since the first harvest," it says. "I have kept the axe sharp. I am tired of keeping it sharp for nobody."

choices.text: Take the axe, and give it back to the herald to carry

effects.log: The axe is very light and very cold. You hold it a moment and hand it back. "Carry it," you say. "Use it seldom." The herald bows lower, and from then on walks a pace behind you, everywhere, and the frost walks with it.

choices.text: Tell the herald to put the axe down and rest a century

effects.log: The herald looks at the axe as if it had never thought of putting it down. Then it does, on the ridge, and lies down beside it, and sleeps a hundred years. That century the frosts come gently.

events.text: The evening star hangs over the west, low and bright, the one the farmers call the dog's supper-bowl star because it comes out when the dogs are fed. The old books say it is the White Emperor's own star. Tonight, for the first time, you can feel it from the inside, the way you feel your own tail.

choices.text: Shine

effects.log: For one evening the supper-bowl star is so bright it throws shadows. Every dog in the land looks up from its bowl. The farmers say it means a good harvest, and it does, because you decide it will.

choices.text: Go on being a tiger on a ridge, watching it

effects.log: You watch your own star come out over the west like any farmer. It is very beautiful. It is very far away. You are not ready for it to be you.

events.text: The Jade court sends for you. Beyond the four directions there is a world where no harvest has come for three hundred years: fruit that hangs green and never ripens, rice that never yellows, judges who never dare to give a verdict, so that nothing is ever finished. "The White Emperor," says the envoy, "is asked to carry autumn there. It is a long way. You may not come back the same."

choices.text: Go, and carry autumn

effects.log: It takes a century. Orchard by orchard, court by court, you breathe on a world that could not finish anything, until the fruit goes gold and the rice bows and the judges, astonished, give their first verdicts. You come home thinner, and lighter, and somehow larger.

choices.text: Send the west wind, and stay with your own valleys

effects.log: The wind goes alone across the dark between worlds and arrives tired. The autumn there is thin, but it comes, and that is more than they had.

choices.text: Ask why heaven let it go unharvested

effects.log: The envoy does not answer for a long time. "Because nobody would judge it," it says at last. "That is usually why." You do not go that century. You think about it every autumn after.

events.text: The autumn rite on the hill, as every year for a thousand years. The mudang is the great-great-grandchild of the child who pulled the white flag, or someone very like them. They spin west with the white fan and the bell and stop dead, facing you. And this time you feel it all the way through: if you answer, you will answer as autumn, and not come back as a tiger. The flag waits. The drums wait. Every ripe thing in the land waits.

choices.text: Answer as autumn

effects.log: You let go of the ridge, the stripes, the stars, the orange wings, the long white body, the name, and go out into the year. The white flag fills. Every leaf in the land lets go at once and comes down red and gold. There is no tiger on the ridge any more. There is only autumn, every autumn, for ever: every harvest your verdict, every first frost your breath. The mudang on the hill, weeping and laughing, is the first to feel it.

choices.text: Answer as a tiger, one more time

effects.log: You come down into the white flag as you did a thousand years ago, a tiger, and the mudang staggers under the weight and laughs, and the village sees you whole. There will be another autumn for the other answer.

choices.text: Let the mudang call, and stay still, and listen

effects.log: Three calls. You listen to all three. It is the most beautiful thing you have ever heard: a human voice calling autumn by its name. Autumn comes anyway, from somewhere inside you, without your having to decide.

events.text: Harvest on the hill, the drums, the five flags, the mudang spinning west. Another year of the rite. The faces in the crowd change every generation; the rite does not. A grandmother holds a baby up toward the white flag so the White Emperor can see it, and the baby sneezes.

choices.text: Bless the baby

effects.log: A cold clean gust, smelling of apples, ruffles the baby's hair. It sneezes again. The grandmother is satisfied. That child will never once, in a long life, lose a harvest.

choices.text: Bless the whole hill

effects.log: Every tree on the hill ripens at once, and the drummers lose the beat, and the mudang, who has seen this before, simply waits, smiling, until they find it again.

events.text: The first snow of the year. You find yourself, without having meant to come, at a den under the roots of an old oak on a mountain with no name. You know it by the smell of pine resin and the shape of the rock. Inside, a striped tigress is curled round four cubs, blind, in a pile, a few days old. One of them is trying to bite the others' ears.

choices.text: Watch from the snow until dark

effects.log: The tigress smells you and does not move. She is not afraid. She just looks at you, a white shape in the snow made half of stars, the way a tigress looks at the weather. You go before the cubs open their eyes.

choices.text: Leave a deer at the mouth of the den

effects.log: In the morning the deer is gone and the tigress is fat and the cubs are louder. Nobody ever knows. That was always the point.

events.text: The magpie is waiting for you on the oak above the old den, the first snow coming down round it. It is not laughing. "Some go to the sky," it says. "Some into a wall, or a cave, or a grave in the snow. And a few, a very few, ask to go back to the beginning: a cub in a den in the first snow, and do it all again, remembering every verdict. It is allowed. It is not encouraged. The old man told me to tell you."

choices.text: Ask why anyone would choose it

effects.log: "To get it right," says the magpie. "Or to judge it all again with the same eyes and see if it comes out the same. Or because they liked the first winter best." It shrugs its wings. "Tigers are sentimental. Nobody believes it, but it is so."

choices.text: Ask whether you would remember the ghosts

effects.log: "Every one," says the magpie. "And the ones you laid down. And the ones you did not make." It looks at you sideways. "That is the cost. And the gift. Think about it."

events.text: Another first snow. The magpie is on the oak. The den below is empty this year, waiting. Behind you the whole western sky is lit; ahead of you is a hole under a tree root, dark and warm and smelling of pine. "Well?" says the magpie.

choices.text: Go into the den

effects.log: You go in, and down, and it gets very small and very warm, and then it is dark, and someone enormous is licking your face, and three siblings are biting your ears, and you remember everything. Outside, in the first snow, a magpie tells the whole mountain. Somewhere above it, the mountain god writes your name down again.

choices.text: Lie down at the mouth of the den, and stay a tiger

effects.log: You lie in the snow at the mouth of the den until it covers you. Then you get up and shake it off and go west. "Next snow, then," says the magpie, which never takes no for an answer.

events.text: An itch between the shoulders all summer, then an ache, then, one cold morning, a weight. You turn your head, which takes longer than it used to, because your neck has grown long, and see them: wings, half-folded, the orange of maple leaves in the last week of autumn. You have seen their like before, painted on the walls of tombs, guarding the sleepers.

choices.text: Open them

effects.log: They open with a sound like a forest letting go of its leaves. The wind gets under them, and you are standing, for the first time, not on the mountain but on the cloud above it. It holds. You were not sure it would.

choices.text: Keep them folded, and walk the mountain one more year

effects.log: A whole year with the wings folded, walking the ridges you know, scenting the trees, keeping the pass. The woodcutters see the orange on your back and think it is a trick of the autumn light. Let them.

events.text: You walk on cloud now as on snow: it gives a little under the paws and holds. From up here every pass you ever kept is a thread, every village a handful of rice spilled in a fold of the hills. You can see the cairns from here, too, the little heaps of stone with a pot turned over on top. More of them than you remembered.

choices.text: Count the cairns

effects.log: You count them all. You know whose each one is. The ones without names you give names, so that at least one living thing remembers them.

choices.text: Walk the clouds west until the sun sets under your paws

effects.log: All day west, over the mountains and the plain and the sea. At sunset you are standing on a cloud with the whole red disc beneath you, and you understand for the first time how big the west is, and that it is waiting.

choices.text: Go down and walk the pass on foot, for old times

effects.log: A traveller coming up at dusk sees a white tiger with orange wings walking the pass road on foot, very slowly, sniffing the stones, and decides to say nothing to anyone, ever.

events.text: A royal army in the plain below the clouds, flying the four-guardian banners on its march, and on the right wing, the white one: a white tiger with orange wings on a field of white silk, stitched by people who have never seen you. The general rides under it toward a war you do not think is just.

choices.text: Fly low over the army, and let them see the real one turn back

effects.log: Ten thousand men see the white tiger of the banner come down out of the cloud, look at them, and fly back the way they came. The army halts. The general, who is not a fool, writes to the court that the omens are against it. The war is not fought.

choices.text: Let them march. Banners are for humans

effects.log: They march. The war is fought. The white banner comes home torn. You watch from the cloud and do not intervene, and are not sure, afterwards, which verdict that was.

events.text: The Western Palace is not one hall but seven, in a line along the cloud like the stars they are named for: Legs, Bond, Stomach, Hairy Head, Net, Turtle Beak, Three Stars. In each a case is waiting, as there will always be a case waiting, for ever. At the end, in the hall of the Three Stars, a beam hangs from the roof beam on a white cord, with two empty pans. It is level. It is yours to keep that way.

choices.text: Walk all seven halls before you sit

effects.log: A whole year, one hall after another. In Legs, a river spirit and a farmer over a ditch. In Bond, a ghost crowd. In Stomach, a famine god who hoards. And so on, to the beam. You sit at last in the seventh hall knowing the shape of the whole west.

choices.text: Sit at the beam at once, and let the cases come

effects.log: They come. They will always come. You hear them in the order they arrive, which is not the order of the halls, and the beam stays level, mostly, if you keep your eye on it.

events.text: A case in the hall of Net: the god of a mountain far to the north has let his tigers be hunted to the last cub for their pelts, in exchange for a richer shrine. The hunters were paid by the size of each tiger and by who struck first. The god does not deny it. "They were only tigers," he says, and then remembers whom he is speaking to.

choices.text: Take his mountain from him, and give it to his shrine-keeper

effects.log: He goes pale under his white beard. His shrine-keeper, an old woman who wept for every cub, wakes as a mountain god the next morning, with no idea how, and the first thing she does is close the pass to hunters.

choices.text: Sentence him to carry his last tiger cub on his back for a hundred years

effects.log: There is one cub left, it turns out, hidden in a cave. He carries it everywhere, feeds it, keeps it, and at the end of the hundred years it is a great tiger and he is a better god, and will not let the hunters on his mountain at any price.

events.text: A case in the hall of Hairy Head, the gathering in white: a funeral procession of ghosts from a battle three hundred years ago, still marching, still in their mourning hemp, because nobody ever buried them and nobody ever told them the war was over. They ask you which way is home.

choices.text: Lead them home yourself, village by village

effects.log: It takes forty years. Some of the villages are gone. Those ghosts you lead to the place where the village was, and they sit down in the grass, and are content. (-10 health)

choices.text: Tell them the war is over, and let them choose

effects.log: Most of them weep, and scatter like seed in the wind, each to its own valley. A few stay, and ask to serve in the hall of Hairy Head. You let them. They make very good clerks.

events.text: The beam in the hall of the Three Stars has begun to lean. Not much; a hair. Somewhere in the world below, every court in the land is a little too harsh this year, or a little too soft, and it has all come up the white cord into the pans. The herald of autumn, or a clerk of the halls, stands beside it and waits for you to notice.

choices.text: Put your own paw on the high pan

effects.log: It comes level. Below, a hundred lenient magistrates wake up feeling, for no reason they can name, that they have been letting things go.

choices.text: Put your own paw on the low pan

effects.log: It comes level. Below, a hundred hard magistrates postpone an execution, and do not know why, and are glad.

choices.text: Leave it, and see what the world does on its own

effects.log: The beam leans for a decade and then, by itself, slowly, comes back. You learn that you are not the only thing holding it, and are relieved, and slightly offended.

events.text: You notice, one year, that you cannot find the edge of yourself. The cold clear wind going over the stubble is you. The red in the maples is you. The weight in the heads of the rice, the first frost on the radish leaves, the geese going south in a line: you, all of it, everywhere at once. On the near side of the year the Yellow Dragon of the centre is holding out the late summer to you, like a bowl handed across a table, and waiting for you to take it.

choices.text: Take the bowl

effects.log: Summer goes into you and comes out autumn. It is not a thing you do; it is a thing that happens through you, as wind happens through a pass. Months later you hand the year on to the Black Tortoise of the north, and it nods both heads and takes it into the dark.

choices.text: Pull yourself back into one body, for now

effects.log: You gather it all up, the wind, the red, the geese, back into a long white body on a ridge. It feels small. It feels like home. Autumn that year is a little late, and very local.

events.text: The harvest moon, the full moon of the eighth month. In every village the families go up to the graves with new-rice cakes shaped like half-moons, sweep the mounds, bow, and eat on the grass. You are in every one of those evenings at once, in the cold that comes up off the ground as the sun goes.

choices.text: Hold the cold back one hour, so they can finish their meal

effects.log: All over the land, families on the grave mounds notice that the evening is warmer than it should be, and stay an hour longer than they meant to, talking to the dead.

choices.text: Let the cold come at its time

effects.log: The cold comes at its time, as it should. They pull their jackets tight and walk home under the moon, talking, and it is a good night anyway. Autumn does not have to be kind to be loved.

events.text: Persimmons. Every year for a thousand years you have not understood them, and now, every year, you ripen all of them: millions, on every tree in every village yard, hanging orange in the cold, peeled and strung under the eaves to dry into gotgam. Somewhere, a mother is hushing a crying baby by promising it one.

choices.text: Go and look in at the window

effects.log: The baby stops crying at the word gotgam. You, the autumn itself, still cannot see what is so frightening about a dried persimmon. You leave, as you left the first time, a little faster than dignity allows.

choices.text: Make this year's the sweetest in a century

effects.log: The gotgam that winter are so sweet that the children are given one each and told it is because they were good. Some of them were.

events.text: After the equinox, in a county town, a magistrate is waiting for a dry day to carry out a sentence, because the law says not in rain, not on a solar term, not before dawn. The prisoner is guilty; the magistrate knows it, and you know it. Every courtroom in the land waits for you, now, to decide when autumn's verdicts may fall.

choices.text: Give the dry day

effects.log: A clear cold morning. The sentence is carried out. It was just. It is the hardest part of being autumn, and you will do it every year, and you will never once get used to it.

choices.text: Give a month of soft rain, and let the magistrate think again

effects.log: It rains for a month. The magistrate reads the case again in the wet, and again, and commutes the sentence to exile at the end, and never knows quite why.

events.text: A tiger on a mountain far to the east, young, striped, very hungry, sitting on a rock above a pass at dusk and looking at a lone traveller on the road below. You feel it the way you feel a leaf about to fall: this is the moment it learns, or does not learn.

choices.text: Send a deer across the road between them

effects.log: The tiger takes the deer. The traveller goes home. The tiger will never know how close it came, and neither will the traveller, and that is how the best mercies work.

choices.text: Let it choose, as you had to

effects.log: You watch. It is a long time. In the end the tiger gets up and walks away up the mountain, hungry. You are prouder of it than you have been of anything in a century.

events.text: A year when autumn could fail. A plague of locusts in the south, a war in the north, and the Black Tortoise sends word that it means to bring winter early to kill the insects. If you hold the harvest back to its proper day, the frost will take half the rice in the fields.

choices.text: Bring the harvest forward a month, in one great breath

effects.log: All over the land the rice yellows in a week. The farmers are in the fields day and night, astonished, and the last sheaf is in the barn the evening before the frost. The tortoise sends one word south: "Neat."

choices.text: Ask the north to wait a month

ok.log: The tortoise grumbles with both heads, and waits. The locusts are thinned by a hard frost at the right time. The rice is in. Everyone is a little cross, which is how the guardians show they have agreed.

fail.log: The north does not wait. Frost on the paddies before the rice is cut. It is a lean winter, and every court in the land is harder than usual, and you feel each of them.

events.text: Every grave on every hill is under you now, in autumn, when the families come to cut the grass. Some of the graves are very old: a cairn with an iron pot on it, a spindle rusted through, a heap of stones on a pass where a traveller died a thousand years ago. Nobody comes to those.

choices.text: Go to them yourself, every autumn

effects.log: Every autumn a cold clean wind goes up the old passes and over the old cairns, and clears the leaves off them, and moves on. It is the least you can do. It is, you think, also the most.

choices.text: Send the shamans dreams of where the old cairns are

effects.log: For a century the shamans of the land go up into the mountains each autumn and find cairns nobody remembered, and sing the names that come to them, and are paid in rice cakes by villages that do not know why they are paying.

events.text: The Azure Dragon is spring now, the Blue Emperor of the east, or near enough. Once a year, at the meeting of the seasons, you pass each other: it going out as you come in. This year it slows in passing, a warm green wind in a cold gold one, and says, "Do you remember the saddle between the ridges?"

choices.text: "Every stone of it"

effects.log: "So do I," says the spring. That year, in one valley only, the plum trees on the left ridge blossom a second time in autumn, and the maples on the right go red in spring, and nobody in the valley can explain it.

choices.text: "Hurry. You are late again"

effects.log: The spring laughs and goes on its way, and you go on yours. Some friendships are only a moment a year, and that is enough.

events.text: The hunger has come up through you like a tide, the old hunger, the one the stars in your coat were supposed to have put out. A lantern on the pass below at dusk: one traveller, alone, singing to keep the dark away. You are on the rock above the road before you have decided anything.

choices.text: Go over the mountain and take a bear instead

ok.log: A bear in its den on the far slope, half asleep. It is a hard fight and a long meal, and the singing on the pass goes on all the way down to the village, and stops at a lit door.

fail.log: The bear is awake. You win, eventually, and eat, and limp home with a torn shoulder. The traveller never knew. (-15 health)

choices.text: Lie on the rock and let the hunger burn until the lantern is gone

effects.log: It goes past below you, singing. You lie with your claws in the rock until the light is out of sight. Then you go down to the river and drink until the hunger is only cold water. (-12 health)

choices.text: Go down to the road

effects.log: The singing stops. In the morning a new ghost walks ahead of you on the pass with a lantern that gives no light, singing the same song, very softly, to keep the dark away.

events.text: Starving, at your age, and the mountains empty of deer after a hard winter. The magpie lands beside you on the ridge with something in its beak: a scrap of dried meat from the shrine at the pass, where a woodcutter left an offering for the old man of the mountain. "He says to eat," says the magpie. "He says he is not hungry."

choices.text: Eat the offering

effects.log: It is very little. It is enough to get you over the mountain to where the boar are. The magpie watches you go and says nothing clever, for once.

choices.text: Take it back to the shrine, and hunt the far valley

effects.log: Three days' walk to the far valley, three days back with a stag. You leave a haunch at the shrine, beside the scrap of meat, and the old man of the mountain, in his painting, looks very slightly amused. (-10 health)

events.text: Even the White Emperor is hungry, it seems. The hunger is not for meat any more. It is for an ending: the whole year leaning toward the frost and the fall of every leaf, and something in you wanting to take the harvest early, all of it, the rice and the fruit and the old and the weak, in one cold breath.

choices.text: Breathe out slowly, a little at a time, all autumn

effects.log: A long gentle autumn, leaf by leaf. The hunger in you eases as the year comes down, and the old and the weak, mostly, live to see the snow.

choices.text: One hard frost, early, to quiet it

effects.log: One night of iron frost in the ninth month. The hunger goes quiet. So do the late fields, and the old people of three provinces say they have never known a cruel autumn like it.

events.text: In human shape you sit in the yard of a county courthouse at night, and the judge, {npc}, comes out in {his} under-robe and sits down beside you as if {he} had been expecting you. "I have a case I cannot hear," {he} says. "Two brothers, one inheritance, and a father who promised it to both. Whatever I decide, I will have killed one of them. They say there is a tiger in the mountains who judges in the autumn. I am asking the tiger."

choices.text: Hear the case with {him}, all night

effects.log: By dawn you have found what the father meant: the land to one, the debts and the friendship of the village to the other, which is worth more, and the second brother knows it. {npc} gives the verdict that morning, and neither brother dies of it.

choices.text: Tell {him} a judge who is afraid of the verdict is the right judge

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time. "That is no help at all," {he} says. "And it is the only help I needed." {He} goes inside and judges, and is not afraid any more, only careful.

events.text: A grandmaster of the murim, {npc}, has climbed your mountain in human shape's footsteps, which nobody has ever done: {he} followed a grey traveller from the market gate to the summit. "I knew it," {he} says, delighted. "The Tiger of Autumn. I have beaten every sword in the realm. I would like to lose to you, once, before I die."

choices.text: Duel {him} on the summit, and do not hold back

ok.log: It is the best fight you have had in three hundred years. When it is done {npc} lies in the snow laughing with a broken sword. "Thank you," {he} says. "Now I know what is at the top."

fail.log: {npc} is better than you expected. Neither of you wins. {He} goes down the mountain bleeding and overjoyed, and you lie in the snow thinking that humans are much stranger than tigers. (-20 health)

choices.text: Teach {him} instead how a tiger waits in the grass

effects.log: A season of lying in the snow together, watching deer. {npc} learns more from it than from any duel. {He} founds no school, but every student {he} teaches afterwards learns to wait first and strike second.

events.text: A heavenly immortal stops you on the road to the Western Palace: {npc}, in robes of white cloud, who bows very low. "You will not remember me," {he} says. "A thousand years ago, a child crossing your mountain at night with medicine for a dying parent. You carried me. I slept on your back. I wanted to say that the parent lived."

choices.text: Say you remember

effects.log: You do, as it happens. The weight, the warmth, the small hands in your fur. {npc} weeps, and then laughs, and the two of you walk the road to the Western Palace together, talking about a mountain that is not there any more.

choices.text: Ask what became of the child

effects.log: "Grew up," says {npc}. "Became a physician. Then a hermit. Then this." {He} gestures at the cloud robes. "It all started on your back." You did not know an errand could last so long.

events.text: An immortal sovereign sends an envoy, and then comes in person: {npc}, ruler of a court in the high heavens, who wants the west. Not to keep it; to own it. "Autumn should answer to someone," {he} says pleasantly. "Why not to me? You would be my White Tiger. My banner. You would want for nothing."

choices.text: Tell {him} autumn answers to the harvest

effects.log: {npc} smiles and goes. That year {his} court's orchards, and only those, drop every fruit green. The next envoy is much more polite.

choices.text: Show {him} the hall of the Three Stars, and the beam

effects.log: {npc} stands in front of the beam a long time. "And if I put my hand on it?" {he} asks. "Then it would lean," you say, "toward you, for ever." {He} takes {his} hand back very carefully, and leaves.

choices.text: Roar

effects.log: The sovereign's retinue is halfway down the sky before the echo stops. {npc} stays a moment longer, alone, to show {he} is not afraid, and then goes, which shows the opposite.

events.text: A human who has climbed to your level, which almost no human does: {npc}, an immortal of the high heavens, sits down across from you on the cloud as if it were a bench in a market. "Everyone up here wants something from the west," {he} says. "I only want to ask if you would be my friend. I have none who are not afraid of me."

choices.text: Yes

mem.note: became my friend at the top of the world

effects.log: It is the strangest friendship in heaven: a tiger made of autumn and a human who outlived their own name. You meet once a century on the same cloud and talk about nothing, and both of you look forward to it more than anything else.

choices.text: "I am autumn. Everyone is a little afraid of autumn"

effects.log: "I am not," says {npc}. "I was born in it." {He} comes back every autumn after that to sit on the same cloud, and in the end you stop pretending you are not glad.
